# Endorsement of Longitudinal POCUS Curricula: An Educationally Valuable Approach to Increasing Clinical Knowledge and Confidence

**Authors:** Blaire K Rikard; Julian T Hertz; Jonathan G Martin

**Affiliations:** Duke University School of Medicine, Durham, North Carolina, USA | Department of Radiology, Duke University Medical Center, Durham, North Carolina, USA | Department of Emergency Medicine, Duke University Medical Center, Durham, North Carolina, USA

## Editor

The use of point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) in medicine has increased rapidly, resulting in POCUS curricula becoming increasingly common. We applaud Crispell et al 1 for developing a longitudinal POCUS elective for medical students aimed at increasing clinical knowledge and comfort.

In the article, “A longitudinal elective facilitates point-of-care ultrasonography education for medical students: An observational study,” 1 Crispell et al demonstrated positive benefits and reception of their elective curriculum. We have also seen benefits at our institution, Duke University School of Medicine, after implementing a similar, but mandatory, curriculum. The longitudinal curriculum spans students’ 4 years.

Institution curriculum consists of preclinical work in MS1, clinical rotations in MS2, a research year in MS3, and electives in MS4. Beginning in the second week of MS1, students are acquainted with POCUS through an introduction session. Throughout MS1, students complete 8 additional, 45-min systems-based, hands-on ultrasound workshops each preceded by a required 30-min asynchronous recorded lecture. During MS2, clinical reasoning POCUS sessions (eg, shock, trauma) are integrated into the Clinical Skills Immersion course. Also in MS2, a required obstetrics POCUS session is embedded into the clerkship. In MS3, students may volunteer as POCUS student facilitators. Students complete sessions in Focused Assessment with Sonography in Trauma and Rapid Ultrasound for Shock and Hypotension and receive training in ultrasound-guided intravenous access and central venous line placement during MS4.

This longitudinal structure provides progressive scaffolding, as students revisit key concepts and apply them in increasingly complex clinical contexts, solidifying knowledge. Engagement is maintained throughout as the curriculum is mandatory. Faculty facilitators are drawn from fields such as Emergency Medicine, Radiology, and Critical Care, all with extensive POCUS training. For each session, faculty receives a detailed Instructor's Guide.

Crispell et al demonstrated an increase in students’ knowledge and confidence postelective and a unanimous recommendation of the elective to future students. At our institution, we found equally positive support for our longitudinal POCUS curriculum regarding clinical knowledge, confidence, and educational value. Our integrated POCUS curriculum was well-received by a recent MS1 cohort and was similarly highly ranked by a separate MS4 cohort.

Specifically, during the 2023-2024 academic year, MS1 students were requested to complete a Qualtrics survey after the first MS1 POCUS session (October 2023) and again after the final session (June 2024). The MS1 survey was completed by 87 students (72.5%) at initial session and 61 (50.8%) at final. The survey consisted of 11 subjective 5-point Likert questions and 12 knowledge questions in multiple choice (6), hotspot (5), and matching (1) formats. For the Likert-style questions, mean perception scores were calculated by assigning values to each response (strongly disagree = 1, somewhat disagree = 2, neither agree nor disagree = 3, somewhat agree = 4, and strongly agree = 5). Mean perception scores were analyzed using an unpaired 2-tailed Student's t-test. For the knowledge questions, all students were assigned an exam score. Mean postinitial and postfinal session scores were then compared using an unpaired 2-tailed Student's t-test.

Compared to the initial knowledge survey (Table 1), MS1s scored significantly higher on the postfinal session knowledge survey (mean 70.2% ± 13.6 vs 54.1% ± 15.6, P < .01). On the opinion surveys (Table 1), MS1s were more confident in their ability to perform basic ultrasounds after the final session compared to the initial (3.70 ± 0.84 vs 3.22 ± 1.00, P < .01) and similarly were more confident in their ability to interpret basic ultrasounds (3.43 ± 0.97 vs 2.97 ± 0.93, P < .01). At both time points (Table 1), MS1s agreed that POCUS was educationally valuable (post-Session 1 mean 4.50 ± 0.68; postcurriculum mean 4.49 ± 0.65) and agreed that the POCUS curriculum should be continued for future MS1s (initial mean 4.59 ± 0.76; final mean 4.52 ± 0.74).

Separately, in May 2024, a Qualtrics survey including 11 Likert questions was emailed to 4th-year students (MS4). Sixty-nine students (51.9%) completed the MS4 survey. Like the MS1s, MS4s expressed strong support for the continuation of this curriculum. MS4s strongly agreed that future medical students should be exposed to POCUS (4.88 ± 0.32) and that the curriculum was educationally valuable (4.68 ± 0.62) and worthwhile (4.73 ± 0.52) (Table 1). Presentation of both MS1 and MS4 data bookends the longitudinal experience, illustrating the sustained value and support across all 4 years.

Expanding on the work of Crispell et al, our findings reiterate the strong educational value of a longitudinal POCUS curriculum. While access to ultrasound equipment may be a barrier to implementation, this challenge is expected to lessen as device prices decrease and more units become compatible with personal devices. Despite these challenges, we believe the integration of a mandatory longitudinal curriculum, over the course of months to years, allows for breadth and depth of learning. Other medical schools should therefore consider implementing integrated, longitudinal POCUS curricula.
